Understanding Eigenvalues

By Ada Lovelace

Eigenvalues show up everywhere in applied mathematics, from vibration analysis to search ranking. This post builds the intuition first and the algebra second, so that the formulas feel inevitable rather than arbitrary.

We will work with square matrices throughout, and we will assume you are comfortable multiplying a matrix by a vector. Nothing else is required, although a little geometry helps along the way.

What an eigenvector is

An eigenvector of a matrix A is a non-zero vector v that the matrix only stretches or shrinks, without changing its direction. The stretch factor is the eigenvalue, usually written as lambda. In symbols, A times v equals lambda times v.

Most vectors get rotated when you multiply them by a matrix. Eigenvectors are the special directions that survive the transformation intact, which is exactly why they are so useful for understanding what a matrix does.

  • Eigenvectors are directions that are preserved.
  • Eigenvalues are the scale factors along those directions.
  • A matrix can have repeated eigenvalues.

The eigenvectors of a matrix are the skeleton on which its behaviour hangs.

Computing them

To find eigenvalues, we look for values of lambda that make the matrix A minus lambda times the identity singular. That happens exactly when its determinant is zero, which gives the characteristic polynomial. Solving that polynomial gives the eigenvalues, and back-substitution gives the eigenvectors.

A worked example in code

import numpy as np

A = np.array([[2, 0], [0, 3]])
values, vectors = np.linalg.eig(A)
print(values)  # [2. 3.]

For a diagonal matrix the eigenvalues are simply the diagonal entries, which is a useful sanity check whenever you implement this yourself.
